name: Variables
description: Learn about Variables and its applications in physics.

content.overview: Quick question: in your experiment, what's actually changing, what's staying put, and what are you keeping an eye on? That's the whole game with variables—some you change on purpose, some you lock down so they don't sneak in and mess things up, and one you measure to see what happened. {{viz:diagram-01}}
content.explanation:
Every experiment you'll ever run has three types of variables hiding inside it. Once you can spot them, everything gets easier.

**Independent Variable** = the thing YOU deliberately change. Say you're testing spring stiffness—the spring type is your independent variable. You're in control of it.

**Dependent Variable** = the thing that changes *because of* what you changed. This is what you measure. In the spring example, that's how high it bounces.

**Control Variables** = everything else you keep exactly the same, on purpose, so it doesn't quietly wreck your results. Drop height, ball mass—lock those down.

Here's why this matters so much: if you don't control your variables properly, you genuinely won't know what caused your results. Maybe the spring got stiffer AND the ball got heavier at the same time—now which one made it bounce higher? You've got no idea. That's the trap. {{viz:formula-01}}

**Let's walk through a real example:** testing how temperature affects magnet strength.
- Independent: temperature (you set it: 0°C, 25°C, 50°C)
- Dependent: magnet strength (you measure it)
- Control: magnet type, distance from test object, time left at that temperature

See how each one has a job? Keeping track of your variables sounds almost too simple to matter—but it's the difference between an experiment that actually tells you something and one that just confuses you. {{viz:chart-01}}
keyPoints: Independent variable = what you deliberately change
Dependent variable = what you measure (it reacts to the independent one)
Control variable = what you keep locked and steady
Control everything except the one thing you're testing
Clear labels on your variables = clear thinking about your results
content.whyItMatters: Without clearly sorted-out variables, your data is basically meaningless—you'll have numbers but no idea what actually caused them. Get this right and every experiment after this becomes way less confusing.
